## 2.4 Caffeine withdrawal

Caffeine withdrawal headache usually begins 12 to 24 hours after a sharp cut in intake and can last two to nine days. Gradual tapering, fluids and simple painkillers are usually enough; it rarely needs emergency care.

Ask about recent changes in coffee, tea, energy drinks and cola. Patients often do not connect a new headache with cutting back a week earlier. A slower taper (reducing by about a quarter every few days) prevents most withdrawal headaches.

## 4.1 The commute home

Twelve percent of respondents said they had nodded off while driving home after a night shift at least once during the review period. Three reported minor collisions. The Trust's car park sleep pods, piloted at Meridian General since March, were used by fewer than one in twenty eligible staff, mostly because staff wanted to get home to children.

## 5. Hydration and simple painkillers

For headaches without red flags, advise fluids, regular meals, rest from screens and a simple painkiller if it is safe for the patient. Paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose on the packet is usually enough. Ibuprofen is not suitable for everyone: people with stomach ulcers, some kidney problems or asthma made worse by antiinflammatories should use paracetamol instead. If in doubt, a pharmacist can advise.

## 3. Burnout

Self-reported burnout rose in every quarter of the review period. By October, 41% of emergency department staff met the review's threshold for high burnout, up from

Across the whole Trust, high burnout rose from 22% to 30%. The rise was steepest among staff in their first five years after qualifying and among those with caring

Burnout and fatigue moved together but were not the same thing. Some staff with high fatigue scores did not report burnout, usually those on predictable rotas who described their tiredness as "physical, not mental" . Burnout was most common where fatigue combined with unpredictability: the sense that rest could be taken away at any time.

retrieved.text:
## Summary

Fatigue is no longer an occasional complaint among the Trust's clinical staff. It is a measurable, rising condition with a direct line to patient safety, sickness absence and resignations. This review followed 1,140 clinical staff for ten months and found that the length of consecutive shift blocks, not total hours alone, is the strongest predictor of how tired staff say they are.

The headline findings:

- Staff working more than three consecutive long shifts reported fatigue scores 38% higher than colleagues on shorter blocks.
- High burnout in the emergency department rose from 29% of staff in January to 41% in October.
- Staff who slept under six hours before a shift were twice as likely to report a near-miss medication error that week.
- Two wards that piloted a compressed rota saw burnout fall by roughly a fifth in twelve weeks, with no loss of patient throughput.
- Voluntary nursing resignations reached 14% over the year, and each replacement costs about four months of salary.

## 1.1 What this review does not measure

The review relies on what staff report. It does not measure fatigue objectively, and it cannot prove that long blocks cause errors. It shows associations that are consistent across sites, departments and months. Where we discuss costs, we use the Trust finance office's standard figures.

retrieved.text:
## 4.2 Saying what advice is

Advice given by phone or chat must say clearly that it is not an examination. Tell the patient which symptoms mean they should come in person.

Good practice in every conversation:

1. Ask one or two clarifying questions before giving any advice: where the pain is, how long it has lasted, and what has changed recently.
2. Give the most likely explanation in plain language, and say how confident you are.
3. Give simple, safe self-care steps.
4. Always finish with the red flags that mean the patient should come in, and say "today" or "now" where it applies.

## 2.2 Tension-type headache

Usually described as a band or pressure around the head, often worse at the end of the day. It is associated with stress, poor sleep, long screen time and missed meals. It does not usually cause vomiting or sensitivity to light.

retrieved.title: Meridian Shift Fatigue Review 2025
retrieved.text:
## Appendix: the fatigue scale

Nine items, each scored 0 (not at all) to 4 (extremely): sleepiness at the start of the shift; sleepiness at the end; difficulty concentrating; irritability; physical exhaustion; headache; change in appetite; poor sleep quality; and "how tired are you right now" . Scores of 18 and above are treated as high fatigue in this review.

retrieved.text:
## 2.5 Medication-overuse headache

Taking simple painkillers on more than about fifteen days a month can itself cause daily headaches. Ask how often the patient takes painkillers, and suggest a GP review rather than more medication.

## 2.1 Short-notice changes

Rest days cancelled with less than 48 hours' notice were the second strongest predictor of fatigue. In emergency and acute medicine, one rest day in nine was cancelled at short notice, usually to cover sickness. In community and day-surgery settings the figure was one in forty.

retrieved.title: Meridian Shift Fatigue Review 2025
retrieved.text:
## 8. Retention

Voluntary resignations among nursing staff reached 14% over the year. The Trust's finance office puts each replacement at roughly four months of salary once recruitment, induction and supervised practice are counted.

The rate was highest in the emergency department (19%) and lowest in day surgery (6%). Two thirds of leavers had been with the Trust for under five years.

Replacing a nurse is not only a cost. New starters need supervision, which takes experienced staff away from patients during the first months. Wards with high turnover were also the wards with the most short-notice rest-day cancellations, a cycle the review describes as "exhaustion feeding exhaustion" .

messages.content: Today's motion: This house would tax sugary drinks. Speaking for the proposition is Amara Okafor, emergency physician and public-health researcher; speaking against is Victor Hale, constitutional litigator.

Taxes work where willpower alone doesn't: price shapes what we buy, and sugary drinks are the easiest place to start because there's no nutritional need for them. In the ER I treat the consequences — diabetic emergencies, heart failure, amputations — and those costs land on all of us, not just the drinker. A modest levy cuts consumption, nudges reformulation, and funds prevention. Victor will call this paternalism; I'd call it paying for the damage.

Let us begin where I always begin: define your terms. "Tax" is a euphemism the proposer is too polite to use. Call it what it is: a sin levy, priced onto the poor, collected by the state, and swallowed by a beverage company that will simply reformulate and repackage. Two points. First, a tax on a substance is not a tax on a behavior; the evidence she will offer is association dressed as cause. Second, a regressive duty falls hardest on the household with the least room to absorb it. That is not public health. That is arithmetic with a moral veneer. I look forward to the good doctor's reply.

Amara Okafor argued that a sugary-drink tax cuts consumption, prompts reformulation, and funds prevention against costs borne by all. Victor Hale argued it is a regressive levy with weak causal evidence. We now move to closing statements.

Victor's regressivity point is real, and I'll grant it: a flat levy costs a poor household proportionally more. But compare it to the alternative we already have — diabetes and heart disease also fall hardest on the poorest, and those costs arrive as emergencies, not receipts. Reformulation isn't a dodge; it's the mechanism working. On causation, no single study proves everything, but the direction is consistent: price goes up, purchases go down. That's enough to act.

The proposer has been generous at the end, granting the regressivity, and I accept it, because it concedes the whole case in miniature: she has admitted her instrument lands hardest on those least able to bear it, then asked us to weigh that against a disease burden she says is worse. That is an argument from necessity, not from wisdom. To what is still open: nothing of substance. The claim that price reduces purchases is not contested; the claim that it improves health outcomes is not shown. A levy can lower purchases and raise revenue simultaneously, and only one of those things funds hospitals. Her mechanism and her premise remain two different claims wearing one coat. On the record, her case proves that a tax is plausible, not that it is just. Ours shows what it costs and whom it costs. I ask you to vote against the motion.
Thank you, Amara Okafor and Victor Hale, for your clear and rigorous arguments on whether this house would tax sugary drinks. The arbiter is now weighing the arguments.
